$comment: What bounds a call, scaled down to a one-second budget, with room enough either side of it that a process descheduled for a few hundred milliseconds under load changes no outcome: the budget is the JS a call runs, summed over its runs, and time parked on a host function is not counted. Each case runs call-budget-plugin.js on a fresh host with `budgetMs` as its call budget and every request answering after `siteAnswersAfterMs`, after one call to `ready`, which pays for the module body, unless the case says `warmsUp: false`. `answers` is the method's answer, or `fails` its error code, and `endsWithinMs` is when the call ends, measured from its start. test/call-budget.test.js walks it through the CLI's engine and CallBudgetRecordTest through the device's runtime (kangzj/yonto#513).

cases.why: a loop that yields to the host between short bursts is cut once its bursts add up to the budget
a call that waits three budgets on the host and then works a quarter of a budget finishes
a loop after a wait longer than the budget is cut one budget into itself
a call that answers with a request still out ends once the request is answered and the work on it has run
work a call left running is spent from that call's budget
the module body's JS is spent from the first call's budget, so 500 ms of it and 700 ms of the call's own is too much
cases.$why: Each alone is well under the budget and the two together well over it, so neither a slow machine nor a thread descheduled across the deadline changes the outcome (found in review of kangzj/yonto#630).
cases.$endsWithinMs: Wide, because on the CLI the first call also bundles the plugin and starts QuickJS, which a loaded machine can take seconds over.
